d.title: What a learner is made of
d.caption: Five pieces, and every algorithm in this course is a different choice of the first two. The last one is the piece people forget is separate: the loss is what the optimiser minimises, and the performance measure is what the business reads — and they are usually not the same function.

d.title: The kinds of learning, by what signal they get
d.caption: The signal decides the whole shape of the problem. Self-supervised is the one worth looking at twice: the label is manufactured from the input itself — the masked word, the next token — which is how a model trains on text nobody annotated.

d.title: The twelve steps, and the classic failure at each
d.caption: The failures are more useful than the steps. Most of them are an ordering error: something that must happen after the split happening before it, or the test set being read more than once.

d.title: How many times each set may be read
d.caption: The validation set can be used repeatedly because nothing is reported from it — it only chooses. The test set is a one-shot measurement, and every look before the end spends some of its honesty, because you start making choices that fit it.

d.title: The decomposition, in four moves
d.caption: Two cross terms vanish, and that is the whole derivation. The first because the noise is independent of the training set and has mean zero; the second because the average prediction minus its own average is zero by definition.

items.label: Substitute y = f + ε
items.desc: the world's output, split into signal and noise

items.label: Expand; the cross term is zero
items.desc: ε is independent of D and E[ε] = 0

items.desc: f-bar = the mean fit across training sets

items.label: Expand again; that cross term is zero too
bias-squared + variance + sigma-squared

d.title: Two thousand fits per degree, and the sum checks out
d.caption: Bias-squared collapses at degree 3 — a cubic can bend like one arch of a sine — and stays at zero. Variance rises at every degree after it. The sum column matches the measured test MSE to three decimals in every row, which is the derivation verified rather than assumed. Meanwhile training MSE falls monotonically and passes below σ² = 0.09 from degree 3 on: the model is fitting noise, and the training error cannot tell you.

d.title: Three conditions that look alike on one number
d.caption: The training score alone cannot separate overfitting from leakage — both are high. What separates them is the validation score and what more data does: an overfit narrows with more rows, a leak does not narrow at all, because the leaking feature is just as informative in every fold.

d.title: Seven ways to reduce variance, and what each costs
d.caption: They are not interchangeable. Only the first adds information; the rest shrink the hypothesis space, which is why each of them can be taken far enough to turn a variance problem into a bias one.

d.title: The fold must match the deployment
d.caption: A fold strategy is a claim about what the model will meet. Get it wrong in the direction of ease and the score is not pessimistic or noisy — it is wrong: 0.995 for a model that had memorised entity ids.

d.title: The six mistakes, and which direction each one bends the score
d.caption: Four of these inflate, and the last two only add noise — which is worse than it sounds, because a 0.03 difference inside a ±0.05 spread is the shape of most false conclusions about which model is better.

d.title: Four kinds of leakage, each with the score it produced here
d.caption: Every pair is the same data and the same model, differing only in whether the leak is present. The second row is the one to remember: a **200-level column of pure noise** scored 0.836 when target-encoded on all rows, and 0.468 — chance — when the encoder was fitted inside the fold.

d.title: What each transform leaks when it is fitted before the split
d.caption: The severity is set by what the transform saw. A scaler learns a mean; a target encoder learns the **label**, at group resolution, which is why it can turn a noise column into a 0.836. All of them have the same fix, and it is one line: make the transform a step in the Pipeline.

d.title: Every family is an assumption about the world
d.caption: There is no assumption-free learner — that is the no-free-lunch theorem stated usefully. Choosing a model is choosing which bias you believe, so the column that matters is the last one: what the family cannot see however much data you give it.
cells: the target is a weighted sum

d.title: In 500 dimensions the nearest point is 86% as far as the farthest
d.caption: Measured on 500 uniform points in the unit cube. The ratio of nearest to farthest climbs towards 1, which is the curse stated precisely: distance stops discriminating, so every method whose whole idea is 'nearby points are similar' loses its meaning. The second column is the same fact from the other side — by 100 dimensions, every point is on the surface.

d.title: Batch, mini-batch, stochastic
d.caption: The gradient gets noisier and the updates get more frequent as you move right, and mini-batch wins because both of those are useful: enough updates to make progress, enough rows to vectorise, and enough noise to leave a bad basin.

d.title: Reading a loss curve
d.caption: Five of these six are optimisation problems with an optimisation fix. The last one is not — a training loss that is fine while validation rises is overfitting, and no change to the learning rate will touch it.
